claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy with nearly equiatomic principal elements and low platinum-group-metal loading.
A post-synthesis nitrogen treatment can incorporate nitrogen atoms into the alloy lattice.
Nitrogen doping will produce multiple metal–nitrogen bonds in the high-entropy alloy.
The metal–nitrogen bonds will be located particularly at or near the catalyst surface.
Nitrogen atoms bond to transition-metal sites and stabilize coordinated metal atoms through a pinning effect.
Nitrogen doping tailors the electronic structure of the alloy catalyst.
Nitrogen doping tunes the adsorption energetics of reaction intermediates.
Metal–nitrogen bonding reduces transition-metal leaching from the catalyst.
Multiple metal–nitrogen bonds improve the corrosion resistance of 3d transition metals.
Nitrogen doping enhances resistance to thermal degradation.
Nitrogen doping will mitigate activity loss under transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO.
Compared with the untreated alloy, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will retain more catalytic activity over repeated operation and aging cycles.
Compared with the untreated alloy, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will exhibit improved durability during thermal aging and simulated increasing mileage.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will maintain low platinum-group-metal consumption.
Nitrogen-doped Pt-based high-entropy-alloy catalysts have shown enhanced oxygen-reduction activity and stability in fuel-cell-related RDE and MEA tests.
The cited fuel-cell evidence does not directly validate performance in automotive exhaust containing H2O and NO or after mileage-related thermal aging.
The proposed mechanism and outcome may not extrapolate to other catalyst systems or high-temperature regimes.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in activity retention, durability, and reduced metal leaching versus an untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
